scope.d: The exact work a project includes, and what it does not include.
scope.ex: Moving the printers is not in the scope of this project.

deliverables.d: The concrete results a project must produce, such as a report, a product or a new office.
deliverables.ex: The main deliverables are a new website and a training guide.

milestones.d: Important checkpoints on a project timeline that show progress.
milestones.ex: We reached two milestones this week.

stakeholders.d: People who are affected by a project or have an interest in its result.
stakeholders.ex: We sent the plan to all the stakeholders for approval.

scope creep.d: When a project slowly grows beyond what was agreed, usually without more time or money.
scope creep.ex: Small extra requests every week caused scope creep.

status update.d: A short report on what is done, what is next and any problems.
status update.ex: I send a status update to my manager every Friday.

blocker.d: A problem that stops you from moving forward until someone solves it.
blocker.ex: My only blocker is access to the shared drive.

ahead of schedule.d: Finished earlier than the planned date.
ahead of schedule.ex: The team delivered the app two days ahead of schedule.

hedges.d: Words like 'maybe', 'kind of' or 'I think' that make a statement less direct.
hedges.es: palabras que suavizan o evitan comprometerse
hedges.ex: Too many hedges can make you sound unsure.

on track.ex: Are we still on track for the June 30 launch?

setbacks.ex: We've had some setbacks, but we are back on track.

bottom line.d: The most important point or result.
bottom line.ex: The bottom line is that we need the report by Friday.

low-context.d: A culture where people say things directly and clearly, so you don't need to 'read between the lines'.
low-context.ex: The U.S. is a very low-context culture.

at face value.d: Accepting words exactly as they are said, without looking for a hidden meaning.
at face value.ex: Americans usually take your words at face value.

follow-through.d: Doing what you said you would do, completely and on time.
follow-through.es: cumplir hasta el final lo que prometes
follow-through.ex: Her follow-through earned her the team's trust.

take ownership.d: Accept responsibility for a task or a problem and act on it.
take ownership.ex: Good leaders take ownership when things go wrong.

article.dek: Why U.S. companies treat planning as a core skill, the five phases every project goes through, and three habits you can use even if “project manager” is not your title.
article.title: From Chaos to Delivery: Why Project Management Builds Success

blocks.en: Every company runs projects: a new product, a system upgrade, an office move. When those projects go wrong, the cost is real. In its 2020 Pulse of the Profession study, the Project Management Institute (PMI) reported that organizations waste 11.4 percent of their investment because of poor project performance.{1} That is why U.S. employers look for people who can plan and deliver, not only people who work hard.
blocks.es: Toda empresa tiene proyectos: un producto nuevo, una actualización de sistemas, una mudanza de oficina. Cuando esos proyectos salen mal, el costo es real. En su estudio Pulse of the Profession de 2020, el Project Management Institute (PMI) informó que las organizaciones desperdician el 11.4 % de su inversión por un mal desempeño en sus proyectos. Por eso los empleadores en EE. UU. buscan personas que sepan planear y entregar, no solo personas que trabajen duro.

blocks.en: The demand is growing. PMI's Talent Gap report estimated that the world will need 25 million new project professionals by 2030.{2} In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics counts more than one million project management specialists, who “coordinate the budget, schedule, staffing, and other details of a project,” and it expects the job to grow much faster than average.{3} And you don't need the title to use the skill: nurses, teachers, salespeople and engineers manage projects every week.
blocks.es: La demanda está creciendo. El informe Talent Gap del PMI estimó que el mundo necesitará 25 millones de nuevos profesionales de proyectos para 2030. En Estados Unidos, la Oficina de Estadísticas Laborales (BLS) cuenta más de un millón de especialistas en gestión de proyectos, que coordinan el presupuesto, el calendario, el personal y otros detalles de un proyecto, y espera que este empleo crezca mucho más rápido que el promedio. Y no necesitas el título para usar la habilidad: enfermeras, maestros, vendedores e ingenieros gestionan proyectos cada semana.

blocks.en: PMI defines project management as applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities, and one of its first steps is defining the project [[scope]].{4} Most projects follow five phases: initiation (why are we doing this?), planning (what, who, when and how much?), execution (doing the work), monitoring (are we on track?) and closing (deliver, review and learn).{5} The plan names the [[deliverables]], sets [[milestones]] on a timeline, and tells every one of the [[stakeholders]] what to expect.
blocks.es: El PMI define la gestión de proyectos como aplicar conocimientos, habilidades, herramientas y técnicas a las actividades de un proyecto, y uno de sus primeros pasos es definir el alcance. La mayoría de los proyectos siguen cinco fases: inicio (¿por qué lo hacemos?), planificación (¿qué, quién, cuándo y cuánto?), ejecución (hacer el trabajo), monitoreo (¿vamos bien?) y cierre (entregar, revisar y aprender). El plan nombra los entregables, pone hitos en un cronograma y les dice a todas las partes interesadas qué esperar.

blocks.q_en: Think about your last project at work or school. Could you name its scope, its deliverables and one milestone?
blocks.q_es: Piensa en tu último proyecto del trabajo o la escuela. ¿Podrías decir su alcance, sus entregables y un hito?

blocks.h: Three habits of people who deliver

items.h: 1 · Define the scope before you start
items.en: Write one or two sentences about what is included and what is not. A clear line protects the team from [[scope creep]]: the small extra requests that slowly eat your time and budget.{4}
items.es: Escribe una o dos oraciones sobre lo que está incluido y lo que no. Un límite claro protege al equipo del crecimiento descontrolado del alcance: esas pequeñas peticiones extra que poco a poco se comen tu tiempo y tu presupuesto.

items.h: 2 · Give every task an owner and a date
items.en: A task without a name and a deadline usually waits. Planning means deciding who does what, by when, and with which resources: people, money and tools. Then you set milestones so everyone can see progress.{5}
items.es: Una tarea sin nombre y sin fecha normalmente se queda esperando. Planear es decidir quién hace qué, para cuándo y con qué recursos: personas, dinero y herramientas. Después pones hitos para que todos vean el avance.

items.en: In Tom Wujec's famous “marshmallow challenge,” teams that build and test small versions early do better than teams that spend all their time on one perfect plan.{6} At work, a short, honest [[status update]] does the same job: it shows problems while there is still time to fix them. Skip the [[hedges]] and give the [[bottom line]] first: are we [[on track]], and if not, what is the plan?
items.es: En el famoso “reto del malvavisco” de Tom Wujec, a los equipos que construyen y prueban versiones pequeñas desde el principio les va mejor que a los que gastan todo su tiempo en un solo plan perfecto. En el trabajo, un reporte de avance corto y honesto hace lo mismo: muestra los problemas cuando todavía hay tiempo para resolverlos. Evita las palabras que suavizan y di lo esencial primero: ¿vamos al día? Y si no, ¿cuál es el plan?

after.subject: Customer portal – scope, owners and milestones

body.t: This project delivers a customer login page and a payment history screen. A mobile app is not in scope.
Luis owns design (due May 9), Priya owns development (due May 23) and I own testing (due May 30).
We'll have a 15-minute check-in every Monday, and I'll send a status update every Friday.

marks.en: Clear scope: what is in and what is out.
marks.es: Alcance claro: qué entra y qué no.

marks.en: Every deliverable has an owner and a date.
marks.es: Cada entregable tiene responsable y fecha.

marks.en: A simple rhythm to monitor progress.
marks.es: Un ritmo sencillo para monitorear el avance.

blocks.en: You don't need a certification to think like a project manager. You need a clear scope, a realistic timeline, and the habit of telling people early when there is a [[blocker]]. Remember Week 1: the U.S. is a [[low-context]] culture, so managers take your updates [[at face value]]. When you [[take ownership]] of a task and show steady [[follow-through]], your plans become promises people can count on. In the case study below, you will see what happens to a team that skips these steps, and to one that finishes [[ahead of schedule]].
blocks.es: No necesitas una certificación para pensar como gerente de proyecto. Necesitas un alcance claro, un cronograma realista y la costumbre de avisar a tiempo cuando hay un obstáculo. Recuerda la Semana 1: EE. UU. es una cultura de bajo contexto, así que los jefes toman tus reportes tal como se dicen. Cuando te haces responsable de una tarea y cumples hasta el final, tus planes se vuelven promesas con las que la gente puede contar. En el caso de estudio que sigue vas a ver qué le pasa a un equipo que se salta estos pasos, y a otro que termina antes de lo previsto.

original.title: Why Project Management Builds Success
original.body_en:
📚 Reading Assignment

Title: Why Project Management Builds Success
Time: ~1 hour

Case Study:
Javier works for a U.S. tech company. His team launches a project without setting scope or clear deliverables. After weeks of confusion, deadlines are missed, and costs rise. Another team defines goals, assigns resources, and tracks milestones—delivering ahead of schedule. Javier realizes project management isn't just paperwork—it's the difference between chaos and success.

Questions while reading:

What mistakes did Javier's team make?

What habits helped the second team succeed?

How does project management build trust in the workplace?

Article Reference:
🔗 Project Management Institute – Why Project Management Matters

Video Reference:
🎥 YouTube – Project Management in Under 5 Minutes — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5d7LXzv3Vv8
original.body_es:
📚 Tarea de Lectura

Título: Por qué la Gestión de Proyectos Construye el Éxito
Tiempo: ~1 hora

Estudio de Caso:
Javier trabaja para una empresa de tecnología en EE. UU. Su equipo lanza un proyecto sin establecer el alcance ni entregables claros. Después de semanas de confusión, se pierden plazos y aumentan los costos. Otro equipo define objetivos, asigna recursos y sigue hitos, entregando antes de lo previsto. Javier se da cuenta de que la gestión de proyectos no es solo papeleo, es la diferencia entre el caos y el éxito.

Preguntas mientras lees:

¿Qué errores cometió el equipo de Javier?

¿Qué hábitos ayudaron al segundo equipo a tener éxito?

¿Cómo construye la gestión de proyectos confianza en el lugar de trabajo?

Referencia del Artículo:
🔗 Project Management Institute – Why Project Management Matters

Referencia del Video:
🎥 YouTube – Project Management in Under 5 Minutes — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5d7LXzv3Vv8

cases.scene: Javier works for a U.S. tech company. His team launches a project without setting scope or clear deliverables. The kickoff message looks like this:

message.text: Hi team! We're starting the new client dashboard today. Let's just get going and figure out the details as we go. Ping me if you have questions!

cases.outcome: After weeks of confusion, deadlines are missed, and costs rise.

activity.model:
Hi team,
Today we start the new client dashboard. Scope: a sales chart and a monthly report page for our top 20 clients; the mobile version is not included. Milestones: design approved by June 6, first version by June 20, launch on June 30. Javier owns testing. I'll send a status update every Friday.
Thanks,
Kevin

cases.outcome: The team delivers ahead of schedule.

activity.prompt_en: Tap the three parts of the update that show strong project habits.
activity.prompt_es: Toca las tres partes del reporte que muestran buenos hábitos de proyecto.

parts.t: Hi Laura, quick update on the billing app.
Milestone 2 (payment screen) was completed on Wednesday, two days early.

why.en: It tracks progress against a milestone, with a date.
why.es: Mide el avance contra un hito, con fecha.

parts.t: Ana and Raj are now on testing, and we're still within budget.

why.en: Resources are assigned: people and money are under control.
why.es: Los recursos están asignados: personas y dinero bajo control.

parts.t: Next milestone: user training on May 15. No blockers right now.

why.en: It looks ahead and says clearly if anything is in the way.
why.es: Mira hacia adelante y dice claramente si algo estorba.

questions: What habits helped the second team succeed?

cases.scene: Javier realizes project management isn't just paperwork—it's the difference between chaos and success. Now his team has a milestone at risk. The manager asks: “Are we still on track?”

activity.prompt_en: Tap the answer you would choose.

options.text: Yeah, everything's fine. Don't worry about it.

Mostly. We've had some [[setbacks]]: testing is two days behind because of a [[blocker]] with server access. I've asked IT to fix it today and moved Raj to help, so we can still meet the June 30 launch. I'll confirm on Thursday.

why.en: Person B builds trust: they share the risk early, explain the cause in one sentence, and arrive with a plan and a date. Person A sounds calm, but if the deadline is missed, the manager will feel surprised and stop trusting their updates.
why.es: La persona B genera confianza: avisa del riesgo a tiempo, explica la causa en una oración y llega con un plan y una fecha. La persona A suena tranquila, pero si se pierde la fecha, el jefe se va a sentir sorprendido y dejará de confiar en sus reportes.
